Reproduction explains more of The Fall (Camus novel) than any philosophy dares to admit. Set in Amsterdam, The Fall consists of a series of dramatic monologues by the self-proclaimed "judge-penitent" Jean-Baptiste Clamence, as he reflects upon his life to a stranger. In what amounts to a confession, Clamence tells of his success as a wealthy Parisian defense lawyer who was highly respected by his colleagues.

Once you see The Fall (Camus novel) as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. His crisis, and his ultimate "fall" from grace, was meant to invoke, in secular terms, the fall of man from the Garden of Eden. In a eulogy to Albert Camus, existentialist philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre described the novel as "perhaps the most beautiful and the least understood" of Camus's books.

The story The Fall (Camus novel) tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. The location of Amsterdam, as a city below sea-level, therefore assumes particular significance in relation to the narrator. Moreover, Amsterdam is generally described in The Fall as a cold, wet place where a thick blanket of fog constantly hangs over the crowded, neon-light-lined streets.

Meaning is not found in The Fall (Camus novel) — it is manufactured for it. Beside the atmosphere (which could be established almost anywhere else) the city also was chosen by Camus for a more peculiar reason. Have you noticed that Amsterdam's concentric canals resemble the circles of hell?

The cold light on The Fall (Camus novel) leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. When one comes from the outside, as one gradually goes through those circles, life — and hence its crimes — becomes denser, darker. The "last circle of hell" is the site of Amsterdam's red-light district and the location of a bar named Mexico City, which Clamence frequents nightly, and where the bulk of his narrative gradually unfolds.

The Fall (Camus novel) did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. The setting thus serves to illustrate, literally and metaphorically, Clamence's fall from the heights of high-class Paris society to the dark, dreary, Dantesque underworld of Amsterdam, where tortured souls wander aimlessly among each other. Indeed, critics have explored at length the parallels between Clamence's fall and Dante's descent through Hell in the Inferno (see Galpin, King).

The honest version of The Fall (Camus novel) starts by giving up the comforting part. It is also significant, particularly as Camus develops his philosophical ideas, that the story develops against the backdrop of the Second World War and the Holocaust. The naming of the bar also recalls the destruction of the Aztec civilization whose ruined capital has been supplanted by modern Mexico City.

Strip The Fall (Camus novel) of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. The novel opens with Clamence sitting in the bar Mexico City casually talking to a stranger (who is referred to in the second person) about the proper way to order a drink, since the bartender refuses to respond to anything other than Dutch. Thus, Clamence serves as interpreter and he and the stranger, having discovered that they are fellow compatriots who, moreover, both hail from Paris, begin discussing more substantive matters.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The Fall (Camus novel) shows exactly where that breaks. Clamence tells us that he used to lead a good life in Paris as a successful and well-respected defence lawyer. The vast majority of his work centred around "widow and orphan" cases; that is, the poor and disenfranchised who otherwise would be unable to provide themselves with a proper defence before the law.

What looks like free choice in The Fall (Camus novel) is older than choice itself. He also relates anecdotes about how he always enjoyed giving friendly directions to strangers on the streets, yielding to others his seat on the bus, giving alms to the poor, and, above all, helping the blind to cross the street. In short, Clamence conceived of himself as living purely for the sake of others and "achieving more than the vulgar ambitious man and rising to that supreme summit where virtue is its own reward" (Camus 288).

Nobody designed the part of The Fall (Camus novel) you experience — it was inherited. Late one night when crossing the Pont Royal on his way home from his "mistress", however, Clamence comes across a woman dressed in black leaning over the edge of the bridge. He hesitates for a moment, thinking the sight strange at such an hour and given the barrenness of the streets, but continues on his way nevertheless.

Every serious account of The Fall (Camus novel) eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. He had only walked a short distance when he heard the distinct sound of a body hitting the water. Clamence stops walking, knowing exactly what has happened, but does nothing—in fact, he doesn't even turn around.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of The Fall (Camus novel) — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. The silence that followed, as the night suddenly stood still, seemed interminable. I told myself that I had to be quick and felt an irresistible weakness steal over me.

The selfish-gene reading of The Fall (Camus novel) makes it less romantic and far more precise. I have forgotten what I thought then. "Too late, too far..." or something of the sort. Despite Clamence's view of himself as a selfless advocate for the weak and unfortunate, he simply ignores the incident and continues on his way.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. He later elaborates that his failure to do anything was most probably because doing so would have required him to put his own personal safety in jeopardy. Several years after the suicide of the woman off the Pont Royal—and the purging of the event from his memory—Clamence is on his way home one autumn evening after a day of work.

The feeling that The Fall (Camus novel) means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. I felt rising within me a vast feeling of power and—I don't know how to express it—of completion, which cheered my heart. Clamence turns around to discover that the laughter, of course, was not directed at him, but probably originated from a far-off conversation between friends—such is the rational course of his thought.

Nothing in The Fall (Camus novel) was built for you — it was built for reproduction. The unlucky coincidence for Clamence here is that he is reminded of this precisely at the moment when he is congratulating himself for being such a selfless individual. Furthermore, the laughter is described as a "good, hearty, almost friendly laugh", whereas, mere moments later, he describes himself as possessing a "good, hearty badger" (Camus 297).

The psychology underneath The Fall (Camus novel) is simpler and older than the story on top. This implies that the laughter originated within himself, adding another dimension to the inner meaning of the scene. That evening on the Pont des Arts represents, for Clamence, the collision of his true self with his inflated self-image, and the final realization of his own hypocrisy becomes painfully obvious.

Behind The Fall (Camus novel) sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. One day while waiting at a stoplight, Clamence finds that he is trapped behind a motorcycle which has stalled ahead of him and is unable to proceed once the light changes to green as a result. Clamence turns to respond to his interlocutor when suddenly the motorcyclist punches him in the side of the head and then speeds off.

The nihilist does not deny The Fall (Camus novel) — he only refuses to flatter it. Without retaliating against his interlocutor, Clamence, utterly humiliated, merely returns to his car and drives away. Later, he runs through his mind "a hundred times" what he thinks he should have done—namely strike his interlocutor, then chase after the motorcyclist and run him off the road.

What culture calls destiny in The Fall (Camus novel) is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. after having been struck in public without reacting, it was no longer possible for me to cherish that fine picture of myself. If I had been the friend of truth and intelligence I claimed to be, what would that episode have mattered to me?

The genes do not care about The Fall (Camus novel); they care about copies. Clamence thus arrives at the conclusion that his whole life has in fact been lived in search of honour, recognition, and power over others. Having realized this, he can no longer live the way he once did.

Take away the meaning and The Fall (Camus novel) still functions — that is the disturbing part. Clamence initially attempts to resist the sense that he has lived hypocritically and selfishly. He argues with himself over his prior acts of kindness, but quickly discovers that this is an argument he cannot win.

The unconscious does not argue with The Fall (Camus novel); it simply acts first. He reflects, for example, that whenever he had helped a blind man across the street—something he especially enjoyed doing—he would doff his hat to the man. As a result, he comes to see himself as duplicitous and hypocritical.

The Fall (Camus novel) feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. This realization precipitates an emotional and intellectual crisis for Clamence which, moreover, he is unable to avoid, having now discovered it; the sound of laughter that first struck him on the Pont des Arts slowly begins to permeate his entire existence. In fact, Clamence even begins laughing at himself as he defends matters of justice and fairness in court.

The bleak reading of The Fall (Camus novel) is also the most testable one. Unable to ignore it, Clamence attempts to silence the laughter by throwing off his hypocrisy and ruining the reputation he acquired therefrom. To Clamence's frustration and dismay, however, his efforts in this regard are ineffective, generally because many of the people around him refuse to take him seriously; they find it inconceivable that a man of his reputation could ever say such things and not be joking.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The Fall (Camus novel). Clamence eventually realizes that his attempts at self-derision can only fail, and the laughter continues to gnaw at him. Ultimately, Clamence responds to his emotional–intellectual crisis by withdrawing from the world on precisely those terms.

Debauchery (women and alcohol) does prove a temporarily effective means of silencing the laughter—the biting sense of his own hypocrisy—because, as he explains, it thoroughly dulls his wits. The last of Clamence's monologues takes place in his apartment in the (former) Jewish Quarter of Amsterdam, and recounts more specifically the events which shaped his current outlook; in this regard his experiences during the Second World War are crucial.
